title: Connected talk
verifiedBy: Fable (Claude Fable 5) — LLM review, authorised by repo owner

rules.text: Each item here is a TURN — two or three short sentences, a question and its answer, or a statement and what follows from it. The per-sentence bound applies to each sentence inside the turn, not to the turn as a whole: nothing gets longer, there is just more of it.

Almost everything in this module is already yours. What is new is the glue that holds a turn together — wa (and), lākin (but), thumma (then), ayḍan (also) — and the small courtesies a turn opens and closes with.

The slogan this module attracts is "Arabic is VSO", and it would have you reorder perfectly good sentences. Both orders are ordinary Arabic, and L1 has been writing the noun-first one all along — ismī Rohān, al-kitāb ʿalā aṭ-ṭāwila. Verb-first happens by itself whenever the verb already carries its subject: dhahabtu ilā al-madrasa ams.

wa is written here as a separate word, which is this course's one deliberate departure from Arabic's own spelling: the script line still joins it (وأشرب). That keeps a turn full of wa costing the word index one key instead of a new one for every word it touches.
lākin ("but") joins two whole sentences and stands at the head of the second one, exactly where English puts "but". Both halves stay complete sentences in their own right.

ayḍan ("also") and qalīlan ("a little") go at the END of what they qualify: uḥibb al-qahwa ayḍan, atakallam al-ʿarabiyya qalīlan. Both wear the adverbial -an this course has been writing since M1's kathīran.
thumma ("then") sequences two actions in one breath: sa-ākul, thumma sa-adhhab ilā al-ʿamal. Each verb keeps its own sa- and its own person, exactly as it did on its own.

Closing and cushioning a turn: maʿa as-salāma ("go in safety") and ilā al-liqāʾ ("until the meeting") are both goodbye; ʿafwan answers shukran; ahlan opens; ṭayyib and ṭabʿan agree. Learn each one whole — they are expressions, not the sum of their words.

A turn is where the register is easiest to break. Everything here is the same spoken-simple MSA the course has used since M1. In Cairo or Damascus you would hear other words for these same turns; those belong in a phrasebook, not in this line.
maʿa takes a person suffix the way ʿind- did in M7: maʿī (with me), maʿaka (with you-m), maʿaki (with you-f). maʿan, wearing the adverbial -an instead, is a different word altogether: "together".

sentences.display: ahlan! kayfa ḥāluka? anā bi-khayr, shukran.
sentences.script: أهلًا! كيف حالك؟ أنا بخير، شكرًا.
sentences.cue: Hello! How are you? I'm well, thank you. (to a man)
sentences.glossEn: lit. "welcome! how your-state? I in-good, thanks"
sentences.literal: welcome! how state-your? I in-good, thanks

words.note: "Welcome" — the lighter, warmer opening beside M2's as-salāmu ʿalaykum, and usable at any hour where ṣabāḥ al-khayr is only for the morning. Another adverbial -an, like shukran and marḥaban; often doubled into ahlan wa sahlan.

sentences.trap: Three short sentences, not one long one. Each half of a turn is a sentence you could already write on its own.
sentences.sound: AH-lan! KAY-fa ḤAA-lu-ka? a-NAA bi-KHAYR, SHUK-ran.

variations.display: ahlan! kayfa ḥāluki? anā bi-khayr, shukran.
variations.script: أهلًا! كيف حالكِ؟ أنا بخير، شكرًا.
variations.cue: Hello! How are you? I'm well, thank you. (to a woman)
variations.changed: -uka → -uki: the whole turn turns to a woman

variations.cue: Peace be upon you. How are you? (to a man)
variations.changed: the fuller greeting instead of ahlan

variations.display: kayfa ḥāluka? bi-khayr, shukran, wa anta?
variations.cue: How are you? Fine, thanks — and you? (to a man)
variations.changed: the short exchange: anā drops, bi-khayr answers alone, and wa anta? hands the question back

mistake.display: ahlan! kayfa ḥāluka? anā bi-khayr, ʿafwan.
mistake.script: أهلًا! كيف حالك؟ أنا بخير، عفوًا.
mistake.why: ʿafwan is the ANSWER to thanks, not thanks itself. Saying it here is like replying "you're welcome" to a question nobody asked: the word wanted is shukran.

sentences.usage: The first ten seconds of any conversation.
sentences.mnemonic: ahlan — "ahl" is family; the greeting says come in as one of them.

sentences.display: hal sa-tadhhab ilā as-sūq ghadan? naʿam, lākin sa-adhhab fī al-masāʾ.
sentences.script: هل ستذهب إلى السوق غدًا؟ نعم، لكن سأذهب في المساء.
sentences.cue: Will you go to the market tomorrow? Yes, but I'll go in the evening. (to a man)
sentences.glossEn: lit. "question will-you-go to the-market tomorrow? yes, but will-I-go in the-evening"
sentences.literal: Q will-go-you to the-market tomorrow? yes, but will-go-I in the-evening

words.note: "But" — it stands at the head of the second sentence, exactly where English puts it, and both halves stay whole sentences. Unlike wa it is never written joined to the word after it.

sentences.trap: lākin joins two SENTENCES. It is not a word for softening a single statement, and it does not attach to anything.
sentences.sound: hal sa-TADH-hab i-LAA as-SOOQ GHA-dan? NA-ʿam, LAA-kin sa-ADH-hab fi l-ma-SAAʾ.

variations.cue: Yes, but I'll go in the afternoon.
variations.changed: a different time in the second half

variations.cue: No, I'll go next week.
variations.changed: answer no, and give the plan instead of the exception

variations.display: hal sa-tadhhabīn ilā as-sūq ghadan? naʿam, lākin sa-adhhab fī al-masāʾ.
variations.script: هل ستذهبين إلى السوق غدًا؟ نعم، لكن سأذهب في المساء.
variations.cue: Will you go to the market tomorrow? Yes, but I'll go in the evening. (to a woman)
variations.changed: the -īn tail turns the question to a woman — her answer does not change: the I-forms have no gender

mistake.display: hal sa-tadhhab ilā as-sūq ghadan? naʿam, lākin sa-adhhab ilā as-sūq ghadan.
mistake.script: هل ستذهب إلى السوق غدًا؟ نعم، لكن سأذهب إلى السوق غدًا.
mistake.why: lākin promises a contrast and then delivers none — the second sentence only repeats the first. Use it when the second half pushes back on the first: naʿam, lākin sa-adhhab fī al-masāʾ.

sentences.usage: Agreeing to something with one condition attached.
sentences.mnemonic: lākin — the hinge that turns a yes into a yes-but.

sentences.display: urīd qahwa, min faḍlika. wa urīd al-khubz ayḍan.
sentences.script: أريد قهوة، من فضلكَ. وأريد الخبز أيضًا.
sentences.cue: I'd like a coffee, please. And I'd like the bread too. (to a man)
sentences.glossEn: lit. "I-want coffee, of your-favour. and I-want the-bread also"
sentences.literal: want-I coffee, from favour-your. and want-I the-bread also

words.note: "Also" — it goes at the END of what it adds to, not next to the verb: urīd al-khubz ayḍan. Another adverb in the -an family, beside kathīran, dāʾiman and ghadan.

sentences.trap: ayḍan sits at the end. English can drop "too" almost anywhere; Arabic parks it after the thing being added.
sentences.sound: u-REED QAH-wa, min FAḌ-li-ka. wa u-REED al-KHUBZ AY-ḍan.

variations.display: urīd qahwa wa khubz, min faḍlika.
variations.cue: I'd like a coffee and some bread, please. (to a man)
variations.changed: one sentence instead of two — wa joins the nouns rather than the sentences

variations.cue: I'd like the tea too, please. (to a woman)
variations.changed: the courtesy turns to a woman

variations.display: bi-kam hādhā? wa urīd qahwa ayḍan.
variations.cue: How much is this? And I'd like a coffee too.
variations.changed: the order grows mid-purchase: the price question first, then wa … ayḍan adds to it

mistake.display: urīd qahwa, min faḍlika. wa ayḍan urīd al-khubz.
mistake.script: أريد قهوة، من فضلكَ. وأيضًا أريد الخبز.
mistake.why: The English seat for "also", out in front. Arabic parks it after the thing it adds: wa urīd al-khubz ayḍan.

sentences.usage: Ordering in two goes, which is how ordering actually happens.
sentences.mnemonic: ayḍan comes last, because what you add comes after.

sentences.display: hādhā bi-khamsa riyālāt. ṭayyib, shukran. ʿafwan.
sentences.script: هذا بخمسة ريالات. طيب، شكرًا. عفوًا.
sentences.cue: This is five riyals. Fine, thank you. You're welcome.
sentences.glossEn: lit. "this for-five riyals. good, thanks. pardon"
sentences.literal: this for-five riyals. good, thanks. pardon

words.note: "Good, fine" — used on its own as the "okay then" that accepts what was just said. Heavy ṭ at the front and a doubled y in the middle. As an adjective it also means good or pleasant, and it agrees like any other: ṭayyiba of a woman.
The answer to shukran, and the same word used to say "excuse me" when getting past someone. It opens with ʿayn and wears the adverbial -an, like shukran itself.

sentences.trap: shukran and ʿafwan are a pair and are not interchangeable: one thanks, the other answers. Saying ʿafwan for thanks is the commonest swap.
sentences.sound: HAA-dhā bi-KHAM-sa ri-yaa-LAAT. ṬAY-yib, SHUK-ran. ʿAF-wan.

variations.cue: This one is five riyals. Fine, thank you.
variations.changed: hādhā → hādhihi: pointing at something feminine

variations.cue: How much is this? Five riyals.
variations.changed: the question and its answer, sharing the same bi-

variations.display: bi-kam hādhihi? hādhihi bi-riyāl wāḥid. ṭayyib.
variations.script: بكم هذه؟ هذه بريال واحد. طيب.
variations.cue: How much is this one? It's one riyal. Fine.
variations.changed: the exchange over a feminine thing — and bi-riyāl wāḥid prices the single

mistake.display: hādhā bi-khamsa riyālāt. ṭayyib, ʿafwan. shukran.
mistake.script: هذا بخمسة ريالات. طيب، عفوًا. شكرًا.
mistake.why: The pair is the wrong way round. The buyer thanks (shukran) and the seller answers (ʿafwan) — swapping them has each person saying the other's line.

sentences.usage: The closing three seconds of a purchase.
sentences.mnemonic: shukran then ʿafwan: thanks, then no-thanks-needed.

sentences.display: anā jāʾiʿ. sa-ākul, thumma sa-adhhab ilā al-ʿamal.
sentences.script: أنا جائع. سآكل، ثم سأذهب إلى العمل.
sentences.cue: I'm hungry. I'll eat, then I'll go to work. (said by a man)
sentences.glossEn: lit. "I hungry. will-I-eat, then will-I-go to the-work"
sentences.literal: I hungry. will-eat-I, then will-go-I to the-work

words.note: "Then" — it puts two actions in order and stands at the head of the second one. Each verb keeps its own sa- and its own person: sa-ākul, thumma sa-adhhab. The th is the soft one, as in thalātha.

sentences.trap: thumma does not carry the future for the verb after it. That verb needs its own sa- — sa-ākul, thumma sa-adhhab.
sentences.sound: a-NAA JAA-ʾiʿ. SAA-kul, THUM-ma sa-ADH-hab i-LAA al-ʿA-mal.

variations.display: sa-ashrab al-qahwa, thumma sa-adhhab ilā al-madrasa.
variations.script: سأشرب القهوة، ثم سأذهب إلى المدرسة.
variations.cue: I'll drink the coffee, then I'll go to school.
variations.changed: a different pair of actions in the same order

variations.cue: I ate, then I went to work.
variations.changed: the same sequence told in the past

variations.display: anā jāʾiʿa. sa-ākul, thumma sa-adhhab ilā al-ʿamal.
variations.script: أنا جائعة. سآكل، ثم سأذهب إلى العمل.
variations.cue: I'm hungry. I'll eat, then I'll go to work. (said by a woman)
variations.changed: jāʾiʿ takes its -a for the speaker — the sa- verbs never change for her

mistake.display: anā jāʾiʿ. sa-ākul, thumma adhhab ilā al-ʿamal.
mistake.script: أنا جائع. سآكل، ثم أذهب إلى العمل.
mistake.why: The second verb lost its sa- and slipped back into the present: "then I go". English lets one "will" cover both halves; here each verb is marked for itself — thumma sa-adhhab.

sentences.usage: Laying out the next hour of your day in one breath.
sentences.mnemonic: thumma — "then-uh": the beat between two things you will do.

sentences.display: hal tuḥibb ash-shāy? naʿam, ṭabʿan. wa uḥibb al-qahwa ayḍan.
sentences.script: هل تحب الشاي؟ نعم، طبعًا. وأحب القهوة أيضًا.
sentences.cue: Do you like tea? Yes, of course. And I like coffee too. (to a man)
sentences.glossEn: lit. "question you-like the-tea? yes, naturally. and I-like the-coffee also"
sentences.literal: Q like-you the-tea? yes, naturally. and like-I the-coffee also

words.note: "Of course" — literally "by nature", and it lives on its own as an answer, usually right after naʿam. Heavy ṭ, ʿayn in the middle, and the familiar adverbial -an on the end.

sentences.trap: The general statement keeps al-: uḥibb al-qahwa is "I like coffee". M1's law is still running, four modules later.
sentences.sound: hal tu-ḤIBB ash-SHAAY? NA-ʿam, ṬAB-ʿan. wa u-ḤIBB al-QAH-wa AY-ḍan.

variations.cue: Do you like tea? Yes, of course. (to a woman)
variations.changed: the -īn ending: the question turns to a woman

variations.cue: No, but I like coffee.
variations.changed: answer no, and lākin carries the correction

variations.cue: Yes, of course. I like tea a lot.
variations.changed: the answer standing on its own — and kathīran turns the liking up

mistake.display: hal tuḥibb ash-shāy? naʿam, ṭabʿan. wa uḥibb qahwa ayḍan.
mistake.script: هل تحب الشاي؟ نعم، طبعًا. وأحب قهوة أيضًا.
mistake.why: Without al- this says "I also like a coffee" — one particular cup. Liking a thing in general keeps the article: uḥibb al-qahwa.

sentences.usage: Small talk over a table, which is where most of this course gets used.
sentences.mnemonic: ṭabʿan — "by nature, obviously": the yes that needs no thinking.

sentences.display: hal tatakallam al-ʿarabiyya? naʿam, atakallam qalīlan.
sentences.script: هل تتكلم العربية؟ نعم، أتكلم قليلًا.
sentences.cue: Do you speak Arabic? Yes, I speak a little. (to a man)
sentences.glossEn: lit. "question you-speak the-Arabic? yes, I-speak a-little"
sentences.literal: Q speak-you the-Arabic? yes, speak-I little

words.note: "I speak" — the same non-past prefixes as every verb since M4: a- for I, ta- for you-m or she — with the -īn tail to a woman, tatakallamīn — ya- for he. The doubled l in its middle is held. The language spoken goes straight after it with its article: atakallam al-ʿarabiyya.
"A little" — the adverb of qalīl (few, little), wearing the same -an as kathīran, its opposite. It sits at the end: atakallam qalīlan, exactly where kathīran sat in M1.

sentences.trap: The verb already carries the I, so no anā is needed in the answer — and the sentence is verb-first for that reason alone, not because of any word-order rule.
sentences.sound: hal ta-ta-KAL-lam al-ʿa-ra-BEE-ya? NA-ʿam, a-ta-KAL-lam qa-LEE-lan.

variations.cue: Do you speak Arabic? Yes, a little. (to a woman)
variations.changed: the question turns to a woman, and the answer shortens to one word

variations.cue: I speak Arabic a lot.
variations.changed: qalīlan → kathīran: the opposite end of the same scale

variations.display: hal tatakallam al-ʿarabiyya? lā, atakallam qalīlan faqaṭ.
variations.script: هل تتكلم العربية؟ لا، أتكلم قليلًا فقط.
variations.cue: Do you speak Arabic? No, only a little. (to a man)
variations.changed: the modest answer: lā, then qalīlan faqaṭ — only a little

mistake.display: hal tatakallam al-ʿarabiyya? naʿam, anā atakallam qalīlan.
mistake.script: هل تتكلم العربية؟ نعم، أنا أتكلم قليلًا.
mistake.why: English needs its "I", so anā sneaks in. The a- on the front of atakallam already says I — anā on top reads as emphasis, not as plain speech. M1's law, still running.

sentences.usage: The single most useful exchange a beginner in an Arabic-speaking country will have.
sentences.mnemonic: atakallam — kalima is a word, and this is the verb for making them.

sentences.display: anā taʿbān jiddan, li-dhālika sa-anām. maʿa as-salāma!
sentences.script: أنا تعبان جدًا، لذلك سأنام. مع السلامة!
sentences.cue: I'm very tired, so I'm going to sleep. Goodbye! (said by a man)
sentences.glossEn: lit. "I tired very, for-that will-I-sleep. with the-safety"
sentences.literal: I tired very, for-that will-sleep-I. with the-safety

words.note: "With safety" — M5's maʿa plus salāma, from the same root as M2's as-salām. Said to the one who is LEAVING, so the person going usually answers with ilā al-liqāʾ instead. Learned whole, like every farewell.

sentences.trap: A goodbye is not built word by word. maʿa as-salāma is a fixed expression, and taking it apart to reuse maʿa somewhere else does not work.
sentences.sound: a-NAA taʿ-BAAN JID-dan, li-DHAA-li-ka sa-a-NAAM. MA-ʿa as-sa-LAA-ma!

variations.cue: I'm very tired, so I'm going to sleep. (said by a woman)
variations.changed: add -a: the adjective follows the person it describes

variations.display: sa-anām li-ʾannī taʿbān jiddan. maʿa as-salāma!
variations.script: سأنام لأني تعبان جدًا. مع السلامة!
variations.cue: I'm going to sleep because I'm very tired. Goodbye!
variations.changed: the same two facts reversed, with li-ʾanna instead of li-dhālika

variations.display: anā taʿbān jiddan, li-dhālika sa-anām. ilā al-liqāʾ!
variations.script: أنا تعبان جدًا، لذلك سأنام. إلى اللقاء!
variations.cue: I'm very tired, so I'm going to sleep. See you!
variations.changed: the goodbye that promises another meeting — ilā al-liqāʾ, and either side may say it

mistake.display: anā taʿbān jiddan, li-dhālika sa-anām. maʿa salāma!
mistake.script: أنا تعبان جدًا، لذلك سأنام. مع سلامة!
mistake.why: The article is part of the expression. It is maʿa as-salāma — with THE safety — and without al- it stops being the farewell and becomes half a sentence.

sentences.usage: Leaving, with a reason so it does not sound abrupt.
sentences.mnemonic: maʿa as-salāma — go with the peace M2 started with.

sentences.display: sa-adhhab ilā as-sūq baʿd aẓ-ẓuhr. hal tadhhab maʿī?
sentences.script: سأذهب إلى السوق بعد الظهر. هل تذهب معي؟
sentences.cue: I'll go to the market this afternoon. Will you come with me? (to a man)
sentences.glossEn: lit. "will-I-go to the-market after the-noon. question you-go with-me"
sentences.literal: will-go-I to the-market after the-noon. Q go-you with-me

words.note: M5's maʿa wearing a person on its back, the way ʿind- did in M7: maʿī (with me), maʿaka (with you-m), maʿaki (with you-f). A preposition takes these suffixes as readily as a noun does — the same machinery as ismī.

sentences.trap: The invitation uses the plain non-past, not a future: hal tadhhab maʿī? is "will you come with me?" — Arabic does not need sa- once the time is already on the table.
sentences.sound: sa-ADH-hab i-LAA as-SOOQ BAʿD aẓ-ẒUHR. hal TADH-hab ma-ʿEE?

variations.cue: Will you come with me? (to a woman)
variations.changed: the -īn ending: the invitation turns to a woman

variations.cue: I'll go with you to the market. (to a man)
variations.changed: -ī → -aka: the answer, accepting

variations.display: lā, anā mashghūl al-yawm. sa-adhhab maʿaka ghadan.
variations.script: لا، أنا مشغول اليوم. سأذهب معكَ غدًا.
variations.cue: No, I'm busy today. I'll go with you tomorrow. (to a man)
variations.changed: the counter-offer: lā and a reason, then the plan moved — maʿaka keeps the company

mistake.display: sa-adhhab ilā as-sūq baʿd aẓ-ẓuhr. hal tadhhab maʿa?
mistake.script: سأذهب إلى السوق بعد الظهر. هل تذهب مع؟
mistake.why: maʿa cannot end a sentence bare — it needs somebody to be with. Either name them (maʿa Rohān) or put the person on its back: maʿī.

sentences.usage: Making a plan into an invitation, which is how most plans get made.
sentences.mnemonic: maʿ-ī — with-me: the suffix does what English needs a second word for.

sentences.display: naʿam, ṭabʿan! sa-nadhhab maʿan. ilā al-liqāʾ!
sentences.script: نعم، طبعًا! سنذهب معًا. إلى اللقاء!
sentences.cue: Yes, of course! We'll go together. See you!
sentences.glossEn: lit. "yes, naturally! will-we-go together. until the-meeting"
sentences.literal: yes, naturally! will-go-we together. until the-meeting

words.note: "Together" — the same maʿa wearing the adverbial -an instead of a person suffix, and it means something different because of it: maʿī is with me, maʿan is all of us at once. It needs no noun after it.
"Until the meeting" — M4's ilā plus liqāʾ, the meeting. The natural answer to maʿa as-salāma, and either side may say it. The final hamza is written: liqāʾ, not *liqā.

sentences.trap: maʿan and maʿī are one letter apart and not interchangeable: maʿan takes nobody, maʿī takes me.
sentences.sound: NA-ʿam, ṬAB-ʿan! sa-NADH-hab MA-ʿan. i-LAA al-li-QAAʾ! — the l of al-liqāʾ doubles, as l always does after the article.

variations.cue: Fine, we'll go together tomorrow.
variations.changed: accept with ṭayyib and move it to tomorrow

variations.cue: Yes! I'll go with you. See you! (to a man)
variations.changed: one person at a time: maʿan becomes maʿaka

variations.display: naʿam! sa-nadhhab maʿan baʿd aẓ-ẓuhr, in shāʾ Allāh.
variations.script: نعم! سنذهب معًا بعد الظهر، إن شاء الله.
variations.cue: Yes! We'll go together this afternoon, God willing.
variations.changed: the acceptance takes a time and the soft tail — in shāʾ Allāh closes a plan, not a doubt

mistake.display: naʿam, ṭabʿan! sa-nadhhab maʿī. ilā al-liqāʾ!
mistake.script: نعم، طبعًا! سنذهب معي. إلى اللقاء!
mistake.why: "We will go with me" — the suffix points back at the speaker who is already inside the na-. Two or more people going as one is maʿan, together.

sentences.usage: Accepting an invitation and closing the turn in the same breath.
sentences.mnemonic: ilā al-liqāʾ — "until the meeting": the goodbye that promises another one.

comprehensionPool.cue: Hello! How are you? (to a woman)

comprehensionPool.display: sa-adhhab ilā as-sūq, thumma sa-adhhab ilā al-bayt
comprehensionPool.script: سأذهب إلى السوق، ثم سأذهب إلى البيت
comprehensionPool.cue: I'll go to the market, then I'll go home

comprehensionPool.display: uḥibb al-qahwa, lākin lā uḥibb ash-shāy
